paras: The lynching of Emmett Divers took place early on August 15, 1895, when masked men took Divers, a Black man accused of the rape and murder of Mrs. J. W. Cain, from two deputies and hanged him from a bridge east of Fulton, Callaway County, Missouri. His body was then paraded in Fulton, shot at, and hung from a telegraph pole at the request of the dead woman's husband. The case ran on the national wire and drew editorial argument in Missouri and in two Black weeklies in Kansas.

Mrs. Cain, the young wife of a farmer near Fulton, was found dead in her home on July 23, according to the Mexico Ledger. Divers, who lived nearby, was charged with robbing, raping and killing her, and the Ledger printed a confession to the killing. On leaving the St. Louis jail, however, he was quoted as saying, "I killed the woman, but didn't intend to. It's a lie that I ravished her."

Fearing a mob, Sheriff Windsor moved Divers to Mexico, Bowling Green, New London and finally St. Louis. After a grand jury indicted him, special deputies J. E. Buckner and J. H. Buchanan went to bring him back for trial. Meanwhile, the Mexico Ledger reported, armed men guarded every road into Fulton and had agreed to burn Divers in the cabin where Mrs. Cain died.

The deputies left St. Louis on August 14 and, to avoid watched stations, left the train at New Florence to drive to Fulton. According to the Auxvasse Review, as quoted by the Ledger, "fifty or more masked men" halted the carriage and took it to the Calwood bridge over the Auxvasse. When the deputies pleaded for the law to take its course, a spokesman answered, "We have wives and daughters to defend." About 1 a.m. the men tied a rope from Divers's neck to the bridge and forced him off.

Several hundred men waiting in Fulton learned of the hanging too late, and the body was placarded "Legal Execution." Later that day horsemen brought it into Fulton in a farm wagon and about a thousand people viewed it at the Court House Square. It was hung from a telegraph pole at J. W. Cain's request, used as a target for bullets, and hung again in front of the Court House.

Coroner Davis's jury found "death at the hands of persons unknown." The disappointed crowd charged that only nine men had done the hanging on instructions from county officers, which the officers denied. Cain told the Fulton Telegraph he was "entirely satisfied." No report of arrests was found, and the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, asked to fund a prosecution, replied, "Not a cent for prosecution."

A St. Louis wire on August 15, carried from Topeka to Washington and St. Paul, called Divers "the negro who outraged and killed Mrs. Cain" and counted more than a hundred lynchers. The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic headlined that the body had been "Saturatd Witn Oil and Burned," though its text described the burning only as planned.

Missouri papers called Divers a "brute" and "fiend," and the Chariton Courier, while regretting the act, held that rape justified people taking the law into their own hands. The Forrest City Times in Arkansas excused the lynchers because they "were sure they had the right man," whereas the Kirksville Weekly Graphic called it a "lynching carnival."

The Topeka Weekly Call, a Black weekly, wrote that Divers deserved the severest punishment but that lynch law should not be tolerated, and that the officers made no attempt to protect a "half witted demented prisoner." On August 31 it used the case against Leavenworth Herald editor B. K. Bruce, who held that lynching would go on as long as assaults did. The Herald in turn reprinted the Globe-Democrat's refusal and a Brunswicker comment on Divers under "Sentiment and Lynchings."

Counts of the lynching party ranged from more than a hundred in the wire to fifty or more in Missouri papers, a dozen joined by others in the Chariton Courier, and nine in the disappointed crowd's claim. The bridge was placed eight, nine or ten miles east of Fulton and the hour at 12:30, 1 or 2 a.m.

reader.title: Lynching of Emmett Divers
bases: A mob took an indicted Black prisoner from two deputies and hanged him from a bridge, then displayed and shot at his body in Fulton (A16, A17, A18).

Divers was hanged by a party of men (counts range from nine to more than a hundred) who seized him from deputies without authority, avenging the rape and murder of which he was accused (A16, A17, A18, A4); the coroner's jury found death 'at the hands of persons unknown' (A18).

Independent Fulton-sourced reports in the Butler and Mexico papers, the Chariton Courier, the State Republican and two separate wires agree on the seizure from deputies and the hanging from a bridge east of Fulton (A16, A17, A22, A19, A4, A6).

accounts.label: St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: A mob of more than a hundred men took Divers from 'Sheriff' Buchanan near Fulton about 1 a.m. and hanged him to a railroad bridge; a thousand men later hung the body on a telegraph pole and planned to burn it in the Cains' house.

accounts.label: Auxvasse Review via Mexico Ledger
accounts.gist: Fifty or more masked men halted the deputies west of Calwood, escorted them to the Calwood bridge over the Auxvasse, and made Divers jump with a rope around his neck about 1 a.m.

accounts.label: Fulton report in Butler Weekly Times
accounts.gist: Over 50 men from the Caldwell area hanged Divers at 12:30 a.m. at the Caldwell bridge, stuffing paper in his mouth to stop his cries; the body was placarded 'Legal Execution' and Fulton crowds accused the officers.

accounts.label: Chariton Courier
accounts.gist: A dozen or more men stopped the carriage about ten miles east, another body joined at Auxvasse creek, and they threw Divers off the bridge; a Post-Dispatch reporter was with the party.

accounts.label: Disappointed Fulton crowd's claim
accounts.gist: Only nine men did the hanging, on instructions from county officers who told them where Divers would be; the officers denied it.

accounts.label: Divers's own words (as reported)
accounts.gist: On leaving St. Louis he said he killed the woman without intending to and denied rape; the Ledger also printed a confession and said he later admitted the rape.

accounts.label: Black weekly (Topeka Weekly Call)
accounts.gist: The crime deserved the severest punishment, but lynch law should not be tolerated, and the officers made no attempt to protect a mentally deficient prisoner.

framing.detail: The St. Louis wire called Divers 'the negro who outraged and killed Mrs. Cain' and headlined 'Feed Their Revenge', 'Lynching a Murderer', 'Met by a Mob of Lynchers'.
Missouri papers called Divers 'the negro brute' and 'fiend'; the Chariton Courier regretted the act but said rape justified taking the law into the people's hands.
The Forrest City Times called it a 'disgrace' but offered in extenuation that the lynchers 'were sure they had the right man'.
The Kirksville Weekly Graphic called it a 'lynching carnival' fit to 'shame barbarism'; the San Francisco Call blamed the Globe-Democrat's stance for future lynchings.
The Topeka Weekly Call condemned lynch law and the officers' failure to protect Divers, while saying his crime deserved the severest punishment.
The Leavenworth Herald reprinted the Globe-Democrat and Brunswicker comments approvingly in arguing that 'the only way to prevent lynchings is to stop the crimes'.
